title: Multiple sclerosis with megacystic presentation: A case report
case_prompt: A 24-year-old man with type 1 diabetes presented with 7 days of posterior neck pain, oblique diplopia, and right conjugate gaze difficulty, which worsened when looking at distant objects. On examination, there was limitation of right eye abduction, left-sided weakness, and paresthesia. Noncontrast head CT showed a 3 cm expansile cystic lesion in the right frontal lobe without surrounding edema or mass effect. Brain MRI demonstrated an oval, T2-hyperintense lesion in the right inferior frontal gyrus involving juxtacortical white matter with an open‐ring pattern of enhancement and multiple perpendicular periventricular T2-hyperintense foci. MR spectroscopy revealed a slight reduction in N-acetyl aspartate and elevations of lactate, lipids, and choline without a significant change in the choline/NAA ratio.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Demyelinating disease with megacystic manifestation was the leading hypothesis — “the diagnosis of a demyelinating disease with megacystic manifestation was considered.”  
2. Infectious process was deemed unlikely — “absence of ring-enhancing lesions with well-defined margins, lack of surrounding edema, and lack of mass effect are characteristics that go against an infectious process.”  
3. Neoplasm was considered but thought less likely — “brain neoplasms tend to compromise the cortical zone, and contrast enhancement usually has an irregular rim-like appearance. In contrast, MS megacystic lesions are characterized by a smooth incomplete rim-like enhancement…”  
4. Other inflammatory or demyelinating disorders (Neuromyelitis Optica, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, sarcoidosis, Behcet disease) were included in the differential — “atypical inflammatory demyelinating disorders may skew the diagnostic impression to … inflammatory or demyelinating disorders (Neuromyelitis Optica, acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, sarcoidosis, Behcet disease)…”
